blocks.text: [II, 574] II. Driven from this position, R. Jonah and R. David devise something else, namely that the Israelites used the dung in place of wood, since during the siege of Samaria they could not go out to gather firewood. This is a little less absurd, since dove's dung can serve in place of wood. For Galen reports as an established fact that dove's dung catches fire so easily that somewhere in Mysia a neighbouring house burned down because dove's dung had ignited spontaneously from the sun's rays. Near that house, namely, κόπρος ἀπέκειτο περιστερῶν, ἤδη σεσηπυῖα, καὶ τεθερμαμένη, καὶ ἀτμὸν ἀναπέμπουσα, καὶ ἁπτομένοις ἱκανῶς θερμή. ταύτης δὲ πλησίον ἦν, ὡς καὶ ψαύειν ἤδη θυρὶς ἔχουσα ξύλα νεωστὶ καταληλιμμένα ῥητίνῃ πολλῇ, θέρους οὖν μέσου λαῦρος ἥλιος προσβαλὼν ἐξῆψε τὴν ῥητίνην τε, καὶ τὰ ξύλα [kopros apekeito peristerōn, ēdē sesēpuia, kai tethermamenē, kai atmon anapempousa, kai haptomenois hikanōs thermē. tautēs de plēsion ēn, hōs kai psauein ēdē thyris echousa xyla neōsti katalēlimmena rhētinē pollē, therous oun mesou lauros hēlios prosbalōn exēpse tēn rhētinēn te, kai ta xyla], there lay dove's dung, already putrid and hot, giving off steam, and quite hot to the touch, and so close to that house, that it touched a window, whose wood had recently been smeared with much resin: so in midsummer the blazing sun, striking from above, set the wood and the resin alight. So Galen, book 3 De temperam. Similar is what one reads in the same author, book 1 De different. febr. and in the book De morborum causis: that the dung of wild doves catches fire more slowly but holds it longer. So no one should think this material wholly unfit for feeding a fire. But truly, who would believe that in the city of Samaria, which, being the royal seat, we may fairly suppose was very far removed from rustic ways, there was so much dove's dung that fires could be built from it? Or that there was anyone who would not rather go without fire for a time than buy so tiny a quantity of a substance most foul-smelling in the flames at so great a price? [col. 40] Moreover, these things do not hang together: that there was a great famine in Samaria because there was nothing to feed a fire with except dove's dung, bought at a high price.

III. The third opinion is that of those who hold that the Israelites bought this dung in order to manure better the fields enclosed within the city, and so provide against famine in the coming year. As if it were very likely that in a most populous city there was so much farmland; or that those who lacked the means to live from day to day had the means to sow; or that the citizens of Samaria were so anxious about the future when they had nothing for the present; or so fastidious in choosing dung that, when other dung, only a little less useful, was available in great abundance, they bought dove's dung at so high a price.

IV. The fourth opinion, equally absurd, is that of Josephus: that dove's dung served them ἀντὶ ἁλῶν [anti halōn], in place of salt. For although I grant that it does not lack salt, yet if they had to use salt from excrement, everyone knows that there is [II, 575] much more salt in urine, and that it is extracted more easily and with less disgust. So there would have been no need to buy at so high a price what everyone had at home. Besides, what would be the point of that salt in so great a famine? If one cared to play the rhetorician, I know that much could be gathered in praise of salt, and that after bread hardly anything is more useful for life: without it a great part of foods is flat and tasteless, can that which is unsavoury be eaten without salt? Iob. VI, 6. Thus, under the Law no sacrifice was without salt, Levit. II, 13. and Marc. IX, 49. And even among the heathen, on the authority of Pliny, no rites were performed without salted meal. So too there is hardly any table of some refinement that lacks salt. But salt also seems to have been the food of the poor. For people of slender means used πρὸς ἅλα δειπνεῖν, καὶ κύμινον [pros hala deipnein, kai kyminon], to dine on salt and cumin, as can be gathered from Plutarch. Hence Diogenes, in Laertius book 6, answered Craterus when he invited him: Ἀλλὰ βούλομαι ἐν Ἀθήναις ἅλα λείχειν, ἢ παρὰ Κρατερῷ τῆς πολυτελοῦς τραπέζης ἀπολαύειν [Alla boulomai en Athēnais hala leichein, ē para Kraterō tēs polytelous trapezēs apolauein]· But I would rather lick salt at Athens than enjoy a sumptuous table at the house of Craterus. And Persius, Satire 5,
You will live content to bore with your finger into a salt-cellar tasted again and again, if you strive to live with Jove.

that is, you will be extremely poor if you are pious. And in Horace, book 1, Satire 3, Tigellius, of whom Seneca speaks in Epistle 126, in order to seem a frugal man, says: I care nothing for the luxuries of the rich,
— — — let me only have a three-legged table, and a shell of pure salt. — — — —
